segs: STUDYING THE SCRIPTURE AS A COMMUNITY
KINGDOM OF COUCHES • CHAPTER EXCERPT
Community is not simply another ministry activity; it is the context
for all ministry activities. It is the environment in which spiritual
growth takes place. And since community is central to our model for
spiritual growth, a few planned socials are not going to get the job
done. We needed a resource to elevate community, encourage it, and
teach it.
Will Walker’s book is probably the best apologetic written for why
community is the matrix for spiritual growth. But the content goes
well beyond theological reasoning, providing extremely practical
how’s and why’s for living out our faith in community. Through
excellent writing and reasoning, personal examples and stories, the
book creates a hunger and desire for communal living.
Content of Book: Why We Pursue Independence; Why We Need
Community; Repentance; Community and the Word-Communal
Quiet Times, Community and Confession; Group Prayer; Godly
Speech and Conversation, and A Commitment to Live Communally.

B I B L E
When my friend John was in college he was invited by a high
school ministry to interview for a leadership position in their min-
istry. John is a sharp guy and had no doubt shown some potential.
The meeting went well and it looked as if John was ready to take
the next step. Then the interviewer asked him, almost in passing,
“By the way, what version of the Bible do you read?” John replied,
“I think it’s the Martin Luther King James Bible.” “Huh,” the man
said, “John, what do you say we do one more semester of training.”
The means by which we learn how to follow Jesus are varied:
circumstances, prayer, contemplation, conversations, and so on.
But central to our understanding of relationship with Christ and
missional community is what we learn from the Bible. This seems
obvious, but for some reason we are prone to get bored with the
obvious. And usually boredom leads to neglect.
I asked a dormroom full of guys to share how they think they are
doing spiritually. The responses varied, but for the most part they
felt like they were not doing very well. They talked about how
they go days and weeks without feeling God’s presence, without
even thinking to pray, just doing life in their own strength. They
said they sort of wake up every now and then and realize how long
it’s been since they felt like they were walking with God. I asked
them to explain what causes them to go into these lulls of flying

on autopilot. They mentioned things like busyness and selfishness,
but nobody contended to really know how things get that way. Just
for fun I asked them how many of them had been reading their
Bibles. The first guy to respond said about two to three times a
week. “It’s two to three,” he said, “because sometimes I don’t show
up to our Monday discipleship group. The other two times are
this group and our large group meetings on Tuesday.” I rephrased:
“How much have you read the Bible lately on your own initia-
tive?” Across the board the answers were in the range of not very
much to not at all. Then I stated the plain truth that was slapping
us all in the face: “You can’t expect to escape autopilot if you are
not immersed in what God has to say about life.”
The written revelation of God must be at home in all methods
of learning. Community is important in that light because we all
interact uniquely with the Scriptures. This is the nature of our
blog community, to write about how the truth of Scripture inter-
acts with the day-to-day realities of our lives. We learn from each
other by partaking of the Bible together.
Most Christians agree that the Bible is important, but in gen-
eral I think our privatized approach to learning what it says under-
mines our respect for it. In other words, what we learn on our own
does not match up with how much we really do value the Bible.
It’s been ten years since I started reading and studying the Bible.
A wonderful lady taught me the method of observing, interpreting,
and applying. She taught me about determining the author’s intent in
light of the historical and cultural context, and how to cross-reference
verses and look up words in the original language. I’m sure I didn’t
even know there was an original language. I was well on my way to
understanding the Bible all on my own. It was great. That is until I
discovered that I had understood knowledge all wrong. I treated it like
something static, contained in some region of my brain where I could
reference it if it were to come up in conversation. This is not the kind
of knowledge spoken of in the Bible. Jesus and Paul, among others,
talk about knowledge as something much more experiential.

I am not opposed to Bible study methods. They are critical to
accurate interpretation. I just think that if we rely solely on our
own ability to execute step-by-step methods, we risk approaching
the Bible too mechanically, too subjectively.
O P E R AT I N G
M A N U A L
Bob was reading a commentary one time and came across this
quote from the author: “God’s operating manual for the human
machine that He created, is the Bible.” I am not going to pin all
of our problems on this statement, but I have heard people refer
to the Bible this way: operating manual, instruction book, survival
guide, and so on. Fortunately, Bob will not let you get away with a
statement like that. He posted this response on the blog that day,
probably that minute:
Isn’t that reassuring? If you run into any problems
with the “human machine,” just consult the “operating
manual” and fix the problem. It’s that simple. Cause
and effect. Problem and solution. But God didn’t create
a “human machine.” He created humans: the crown
jewels of His creation, the ones who bear His own
image. If we were machines, life would be a lot easier.
The fact that we’re not is what makes life confusing
and complex. (Sometimes I wish my wife were simply a
‘human machine.’ Then I could consult the ‘operating
manual’ and figure her out.) Apparently the “biblical
scholar” (phrase used loosely) who wrote the article
has never pondered the books of Ecclesiastes, Job, or
Psalms. It’s hard to see exactly how those books fit in
the “operating manual.” Reading his quote made me
remember how much I hate simplistic, formula-driven
Christianity. The Bible is not God’s “operating manual
for the human machine.” It is the story of God’s interac-
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
tion with humankind. It is a complex, layered, intense
portrait of God’s goodness and our brokenness. It is the
cosmic drama of redemption that is being worked out
in history, with the end goal of God being glorified in
all the earth, gathering worshipers for Himself from
every tribe and tongue and nation. Heaven will not
be a warehouse of human machines, but a community
of redeemed human beings. Father, forgive the simple
scholars, for they know not what they obscure.
I told you, Bob’s a preacher. We love that about him. The funny
thing is, I suspect Bob secretly aspires to be a scholar himself.
C O M P L E X I T Y
Nobody reads operating manuals for pleasure, because they tend
to be boring. Brett gets the impression that some of the students we
meet with find the Bible boring. They only read it because they are
supposed to or because they need to find a solution of some sort.
Very few read the Bible because they long to discover the depth of
mystery that is God and man and relationship between the two.
One day at Peet’s Coffee, Brett and I were talking about the
Gutenberg press and how our methods of Bible study were hardly
possible for the first fifteen centuries of the church. Old and New
Testament Christians did not read the Bible. They heard it from
those who knew the stories or had the letters. This doesn’t mean
that we shouldn’t read it, of course, but perhaps there is some-
thing to simply reading it aloud instead of jumping head first into
“study.” Maybe this is why, even after his articulate letters, Paul
still expressed desires like, “I long to see you, so that I may impart
to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you, that is, that we may be
mutually comforted by one another’s faith, both yours and mine.”1

This is a post Brett wrote about his experimentation in reading
the Bible aloud with students:
The other night I watched the movie Primer with
several friends. Primer is not an easy movie to under-
stand; in fact, I left quite unsettled. It all came at me a
bit too fast, without the proper narrator asides or flash-
backs to let me know what was really going on. Just
tension. The kind of tension that leads the nocturnal
nerd in me to read posts on message boards from equally
curious people with far more time on their hands. As I
began to read plot analysis and scene by scene break-
downs, I started to feel a sense of loss. In attempting to
understand every detail, I found myself understanding
the movie’s point less and less. Dissecting a frog can
be helpful in figuring out its inner workings, but it also
tends to kill it.
I sometimes wonder if our attempts at dissecting the
Bible are the same way—bringing a sense of knowledge
while removing all of the life. You’ve heard it said that
God’s Word is living and active, sharper than any two-
edged sword.2 This sounds mysterious, exciting, a bit
unsettling. It makes me want to read the Bible a lot
more than I do. Of course, it also makes me want to
look up a verse on peace or understanding in the index
at the back so I can diffuse those emotions and move
on with my day.
When I look at the Bible, I see a series of books
and letters important enough to be copied for years by
hand, letter by letter. Words pregnant with mystery and
understanding, life and death. Stories, poetry, proph-
ecy, heartfelt asides between apostles and churches.
2 Hebrews 4:12
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
Quite meaningful really. Then I look at the veritable
textbook of a Bible I have sitting on my shelf: full of
crossreferences, clear interpretations of confusing pas-
sages, and a concordance for looking up every men-
tion of the word “recompense.” I think this reflects
the importance of the Bible, I’m just not sure it retains
the meaning of it. Great, valuable thought has gone
into understanding this great, valuable book; it’s just
that this wealth of information makes my own need to
know seem much less valuable. Dissecting a poem will
help you understand it, but handing all of these inter-
pretations to someone else will not help them love it.
Over the past few weeks, a friend and I have been
getting together to read Luke’s Gospel. We’ll head
over toSpider House, grab some coffee and a table, and
start reading. Out loud. He reads for a bit, and then I’ll
read for a bit. We’ll stop every now and then to talk
about what we find fascinating or what we don’t under-
stand or what we’ve never noticed before. Often we’ll
be reminded of events taking place in our own lives.
Occasionally we’ll stop and pray.
Reading Luke’s words about Jesus and His message,
I am refreshed and challenged, even though I’m some-
times left a bit confused. (It’s coming at me a little fast,
without the proper flashbacks or plot analysis.) I feel this
urge to get out a commentary, but I avoid it. The tension
I feel pushes me to keep reading, to understand more. I
find myself not only reading things that are true, but I
also find this truth to be full of emotion and meaning.
It feels very much worth believing. I am amazed at the
faith of Zacharias and of Mary and of the Roman centu-
rion, surprised at what their trust in God says about my
own. I love seeing Jesus’ clear sense of mission coupled
with His demonstrative love of individual people.
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
I suppose we’re reading the Bible as literature, noth-
ing extraordinary. Though in reading its words in con-
text, and without Cliff Notes, it’s impossible to escape
how much more than literature—or a textbook on
life—the Bible really is. Maybe the reason people have
a hard time picking up the Bible is because someone
else has already picked it apart.
T H E
C O M M U N A L
Q U I E T
T I M E
My intention is not to diminish the value of methods or to vilify
scholarship. My sincere hope is to stir something inside you that
moves you to read the Bible afresh, to implore others to join you,
to pursue truth and meaning with the aim of finding life in the
person of Jesus.
So where does the Bible fit into spiritual life? For most people it
fits into what they have come to call “quiet times.” I was taught to
have quiet times, first as a child in the corner, and then as an adult
at the coffee shop. Both are wonderful and should be treasured
as part of the American way of life. What I don’t understand,
though, is how the Bible got mixed up with quiet times the way it
did. Never have two simple words so shaped the way people think
about what it means to study the Bible, or to be a Christian for
that matter. The approach has become common, even prescrip-
tive:
1. Find a quiet place, maybe some music in the back-
ground, coffee/tea, comfy chair, etc.
Read something in the Bible. Read for at least fifteen
minutes (this seems to be the minimum requirement).
3. If you have questions get them answered immedi-
ately by reading a commentary (warning: reading mul-
tiple commentaries will only lead to more questions).
4. Journal and/or pray.
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
5. Impress someone with what you have learned
(optional, and for experienced Christians only).
This would by most standards be considered a good approach
to Bible study. That it may be, but it is not the best approach to
learning. I am biased, of course, because I fail miserably at the
whole quiet time agenda. It’s been awhile since I have read the
Bible this way: privately, quietly, devotionally. I have read and
discussed it with people, read it to prepare for talks and small
groups, written about some of its passages and ideas, and read a
few complimentary books along the way. So either I am not a good
Christian or it is possible to learn the Bible and love Jesus/people
apart from this approach. Perhaps both are true.
It seems to me that the Bible is meant to be read aloud, heard
in community, talked about at dinner, applied to actual life,
debated—anything but confined to the comfy recesses of my
“devotional life.” I am not suggesting that we should not read
the Bible alone. My friend Jonathan points out the dangers of
throwing out personal reading: “Personal choice and discipline
are critical for cultivating intimacy with the Lord whenever one is
apart from the community.
If this discipline is not developed, the
community will become a crutch and not a catapult in the aim for
holy living.” If you benefit from personal Bible study, don’t neglect
it. I am just saying that if devotional reading is your only approach
to learning the Bible, you will likely be disappointed with the
results.
I like to read. I like to talk about how I like to read more than
I like to read, but nevertheless I manage to read some books now
and then. Last year I read Renovation of the Heart by Dallas Wil-
lard. I enjoyed it so much that I recommended it to all my friends.
Seeing my enthusiasm, they asked, “What’s it about?” This is the
point when I realized that I couldn’t articulate much once I got
past the very obvious. It was terrifically meaningful when I read it,
but somehow it lost its place in my mind and life. This happens
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
a lot. I’m always assuming that I understand what I read, and it
isn’t until I have to talk about it that I see how much I still don’t
understand. I expect the same goes for stuff we have read in quiet
times past.
Just the other day I was leading a discussion and trying to write
down what someone had said. I knew what she was saying, but
when I tried to capture it in writing, I got stuck. I just wrote down,
“the thing that Melinda said,” and told the group I would know
what that meant when I typed up the notes. Seizing the opportu-
nity to make me live by my own advice, Jeremy said, “If you can’t
say it, you probably don’t know it.” So we kept talking about the
idea until we could articulate it; that is, until I could see that I
really didn’t understand what I thought I knew. All I am saying is
that people see things differently, and when we talk about what
we know, we allow others to show us a new perspective, and vice
versa. Solomon said it this way: “He who states his case first seems
right, until the other comes and examines him.”3
Paul wrote to the Colossians about learning and understand-
ing spiritual truth. He said, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you
richly.”4 That verse, read alone, would seem to promote devotional
reading. But the context indicates that both the means by which
we let the word dwell and the purpose for letting the word dwell
are overtly relational and communal:
Therefore, as God’s chosen people, holy and dearly
loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness,
humility, gentleness and patience. Bear with each other
and forgive whatever grievances you may have against
one another. Forgive as the lord forgave you. And
over all these virtues put on love, which binds them
all together in perfect unity. Let the peace of Christ
rule in your hearts, since as members of one body you
3 Proverbs 18:17, NIV; 4 Colossians 3:16, NIV
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
were called to peace. And be thankful. Let the word of
Christ dwell in you richly as you teach and admonish
one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms,
hymns and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts
to God.5
This sounds more like group therapy or even a wild party than a
quiet corner in the coffee shop. If the only place the Bible gets to
“dwell” in your life is your quiet time—not in your conversations
and communities—I think you might be surprised at how much
assumed understanding you have and, quite frankly, how boring
the Bible has become to you.
You may still be asking why you can’t learn in private. I didn’t
really say that. Knowledge is multi faceted, and what I am saying is
that the highest priority knowledge—experiential knowledge—is
what is inseparable from community. You can have quiet times
that are neat and tidy with, “one thing you could do today to apply
what you learned.” This is a legitimate means of learning. I don’t
do this very much anymore because there is too much assumed
understanding and not enough frustration or opportunity to be
wrong. It’s too packaged and pleasant to affect actual life.
Some of us argue that we need time to get our thoughts
together. That’s fine, but I wonder if what we really mean is that
we need time to get our act together. Honest contemplation (get-
ting our thoughts together) depends on our ability to distinguish
between God’s voice and our own thoughts. That is why we need
to invite other people into the process, because we can’t see our
own face. We need people to ask us questions, impose their views
and experiences on our understanding of things, challenge our
complacency, encourage our growth, force us to articulate our
thoughts, enable us to see ourselves in ways that we could never
see on our own.
5 Colossians 3:12-16, NIV

In reality, learning is probably an organic process. We contem-
plate, we process with others, and we contemplate again, always
refining. What has been gutted from the process is the communal
hearing, learning, and processing of the Word. We practice Chris-
tianity the same way we go to school—we study on our own and
come in and take a test. It’s a lousy model for Christian growth
and, incidentally, a pretty lousy academic model as well.
Our spiritual climate is dominated by a privatized mindset with
regard to learning and growing: self-help, devotionals, quiet times,
and the phenomenon that I can go to church and not have to
talk to anyone. To turn the whole quiettime approach on its head,
I propose something quite revolutionary. I offer to you the TV
devotional, wherein you get up every morning to snuggle up on
the couch and spend an hour or so watching your favorite shows
(TIVO makes this all possible). Then, during the rest of the day
when you would normally watch and talk about TV with other
people, you could read and talk about the Bible, especially as it
interacts with your actual life. I call this the communal quiet time.
An evening might be spent with family or friends reading and
talking about Scripture, contemplating and cross-examining the
ideas, allowing biblical truth to dwell in your community. I am
not opposed to being alone or taking time to read, reflect, or pray.
I just think that the Bible speaks to us generally noisier than our
quiet times will permit.
E X P E R I M E N T S
W I T H
C O M M U N A L
Q U I E T
T I M E S
Communal quiet times are not complicated. You just need a
Bible and at least one other person. Getting started is the hardest
part, which is true about every kind of discipline.
When Debbie and I started doing this together, we decided that
we would not have any agenda for discussion. We just took turns
reading aloud 1 John. We talked about a few things we noticed
as we went, but mostly we just enjoyed sharing in the reading
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
of Scripture together. We haven’t read anything since then, not
because we didn’t benefit from it, but because habits are hard to
form. Sometimes you have to get started several times. Again, you
will get frustrated if you want relationships to get better. Reading
aloud together is merely a simple exercise that will help you jump-
start meaningful conversations.
Brett and I work on a lot of small group materials, so we discuss
passages with a very specific agenda of getting to the core issues
and figuring out how to help others get there too. Usually we read
a passage and start talking about the stuff that jumps out at us,
things we find interesting, suspect to be important, or have ques-
tions about. We often find that we read the same verses in very
different ways. That is why multiple perspectives are so important
to learning. Sometimes we try to articulate what the passage com-
municates in one simple sentence. This forces us to read for under-
standing. You would learn a lot just by trying that with people.
The ideas in Scripture that have had the most profound impact on
me are from passages that Brett and I have discussed in this way,
including the ideas in Philippians that I wrote about in chapter 1.
Brett and I found communal quiet times to be so helpful that
we wanted to try it out with a group of students. We asked them
to pick a number between one and twenty-seven (there are
twenty-seven books in the New Testament). Once they picked the
number, we turned to that book and asked them to pick a number
between one and however many chapters were in that book. We
figured between the two of us we would be familiar enough with
the “randomly” selected passage to wing a good discussion. But the
lot was cast to 2 John. Neither of us had ever read 2 John. I’m not
sure I even knew there was a 2 John.
We began by reading the passage aloud, and then we asked
people to share their first impressions—Not interpretations, just
stuff they noticed. After that we had everyone write down five
questions that, if they could have answered, would help them
understand what the passage talked about. They wanted to know,
© 2010, CruPress, All Rights Reserved. CruPress.com
of course, who the “chosen lady and her children” were and if
the “dear lady” was the same person, not to mention the “chosen
sister.” There were also questions about the antichrist reference
and what it meant that they could lose what they had worked for.
The weirdness of this passage gives you an idea of how we were
able to spend an hour talking about people’s questions and trying
as a group to find answers. I was shocked by how insightful the
discussion was and by how much I learned. I left feeling very sober
about the need to endure in the work of loving people. We had
similar discussions with other groups about various passages and/or
topics, all of which were personally and communally stimulating.
Once you have the framework in place, I suppose there are
dozens of ways to have a communal quiet time. Again, the ele-
ments are simple: people, a Bible, and a desire to learn in such
a way that the ideas become meaningful in actual life. Execu-
tion, however, is not always easy. Our conversational habits and
personal insecurities sometimes make simple communication and
learning more complex. In spite of all the talking we do—maybe
because of all the talking we do—we tend to forget the value and
power of words. We need to think more intentionally about the
role of conversation in personal growth and in the life of com-
munity.
Most people do not think of conversation as a spiritual disci-
pline, but we think conversation might be the most practical and
fruitful discipline at our disposal. That’s why we devoted the next
chapter to it.
